title: Compose performance & diagnosis
scopeHtml: Measuring and fixing Compose performance: Layout Inspector counts, compiler reports, tracing, baseline profiles, release-vs-debug, trap catalogue, benchmarks. Version notes: strong skipping is default from Kotlin 2.0.20; runtime-tracing composition tracing needs API 30+ (recomposition tracing needs runtime-tracing 1.13+, verify against your BOM).

questions.promptHtml: What do the recomposition and skip counts in Layout Inspector tell you, and what don't they tell you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you use the tool as a hint generator or mistake counts for a performance verdict.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Layout Inspector shows, per composable, how many times it recomposed and how many times Compose skipped it since you last reset. A high recompose count on something that shouldn't change is a lead. But counts are not time: a composable recomposing 300 times for 20 microseconds each is fine, and skipping isn't free either. I confirm with a trace or Macrobenchmark before changing code.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compose records, for each recomposition scope, whether the scope re-executed or was skipped because its inputs were equal. Layout Inspector (connected to a debuggable app) reads these counters and shows them in the tree. You can reset counts, perform the interaction (scroll, type), and read the delta.

What a count can answer: "Is this node recomposing when nothing it displays changed?" That points at unstable inputs, a state read too high, or a new lambda per pass. What it cannot answer: how long each pass took, whether the work landed in the frame deadline, or whether recomposition was even the bottleneck (layout and draw are separate phases).

The official docs say explicitly that skipping costs something: parameters are stored in the slot table and compared on each pass, and an expensive equals() on a skipped composable can cost more than recomposing a cheap one. So "make every count zero" is an anti-goal.

Interaction -> reset counts -> repeat 10x -> read deltas
Recompose = 10 on a leaf Text that shows static data  -> investigate
Recompose = 10 on the row whose data really changed   -> expected

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a (tooling).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Measuring on a debug build and drawing conclusions about frame time.
  • Treating "skipped" as free and "recomposed" as bad.
  • Forgetting that inline containers (Row, Column, Box) are not scopes, so the count appears on the enclosing function.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can the counter show a parent recomposing when only a child's state changed? → Only if the parent itself read that state; otherwise only the child scope should count.
  2. How do you see which state caused it? → Recomposition tracing in a system trace (runtime-tracing 1.13+, verify), or reasoning from reads.
  3. Do counts help for layout/draw cost? → No; use trace sections (Layout, draw) and Perfetto.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Look for big numbers and fix them." Senior: counts are a hypothesis generator; the verdict is frame time from a trace or benchmark, and the fix often moves a read to layout/draw rather than adding skipping.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent a sprint making a header skippable (count 40 to 0) with no change in p95 frame time, because the real cost was an offset read in composition on a different node.

questions.promptHtml: Why is a Compose app so much slower in a debug build, and how should you profile it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common junior mistake is "Compose is janky" based on a debug APK.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Debug builds are not optimized: no R8 shrinking/optimization, the app is debuggable so ART runs more in interpreter/JIT with debugging overhead, and Compose's own code isn't AOT-compiled by a baseline profile. Compose is a library, so its code is loaded and JIT-compiled at runtime. I always measure on a release-like build: minified, non-debuggable, profileable, with a baseline profile, on a real mid-tier device.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compose ships as library code, not part of the platform image, so on first use it is interpreted/JIT-compiled unless a baseline profile gives ART an AOT-compilation hint. The docs state the Compose artifacts ship a default profile, but it covers only Compose library code, not your composables.

Debug adds: debuggable=true (limits ART optimizations), no R8 (dead code and inlining left in), extra checks and, with tooling attached, instrumentation. Result: first-scroll stutter and long frames that vanish in release.

Profiling setup: a release build type variant (often named benchmark) that is isMinifyEnabled = true, signed with the debug key, isDebuggable = false, and a <profileable android:shell="true"/> manifest entry so profilers can attach.

// app/build.gradle.kts
buildTypes {
    create("benchmark") {
        initWith(getByName("release"))
        signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")
        matchingFallbacks += listOf("release")
        isDebuggable = false
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Benchmarking in an emulator or on a flagship only.
  • Measuring a release build without a baseline profile and concluding "R8 didn't help".
  • Shipping composition-tracing strings by accident (they are added by the compiler; strip with the documented Proguard rule if size matters).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Compose itself slow, then? → No; the debug gap is mostly missing AOT and R8, not the runtime design.
  2. Why do Macrobenchmarks require a non-debuggable target? → Debuggable skews timings and prevents proper compilation modes.
  3. What does CompilationMode control? → How much of the app is precompiled before the benchmark (None, Partial with baseline profile, Full); it lets you quantify a profile's benefit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use release build." Senior: names the specific causes (JIT of library code, no R8, debuggable), sets up a profileable benchmark variant, and sets the device tier explicitly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team rewrote a settings list because of "jank" that only existed in debug; the release build with a baseline profile was already within budget.

questions.promptHtml: How do you generate and read Compose compiler reports, and when are they worth the effort?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can see skippability and stability facts, not guess at them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I enable reportsDestination and metricsDestination in the composeCompiler Gradle block and build a release variant. I get *-classes.txt (stability of classes), *-composables.txt (restartable/skippable and per-parameter stability) and a CSV. I use them only when I have a measured recomposition problem, to see why a composable isn't skipping, not to chase 100% skippable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
// module build.gradle.kts
composeCompiler {
    reportsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_compiler")
    metricsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_compiler")
}

Run on a release build (docs insist, results differ otherwise). Output reading:

restartable skippable fun SnackCollection(
  stable snackCollection: SnackCollection
  stable onSnackClick: Function1<Long, Unit>
)
restartable fun HighlightedSnacks(unstable snacks: List<Snack>)   // not skippable pre strong skipping
unstable class Snack { unstable val tags: Set<String> }

With strong skipping (default since Kotlin 2.0.20), restartable composables become skippable even with unstable params; unstable params are compared by ===, stable by equals(). So the useful signal changes: not "is it skippable?" but "is a new instance allocated every pass for an unstable param?"

Workflow: build report -> find the composable that the trace/Layout Inspector flagged -> read its params -> check class report for the unstable field -> fix at source (stable instance reuse, @Immutable on a small flat class, stability config for third-party types, wrapper).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running on debug.
  • Enabling reports for the whole repo and trying to make everything skippable.
  • Reading reports from a module that lacks the compose plugin (classes there show as unstable by inference rules, not by contract).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is stability_config.conf? → Compiler-time list of classes to treat as stable (Compose compiler 1.5.5+); you take responsibility for the contract.
  2. Does <runtime stability> = Unstable mean it never skips? → Under strong skipping it skips on ===.
  3. How do you keep it from rotting? → Diff composables.csv in CI for hot-path composables (see the CI gate question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Look for unstable and add @Immutable." Senior: re-frames the reports for strong skipping, warns against annotating collection-holding models (per-element equals()), and ties every change to a benchmark.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A report showed LocalDateTime-holding models unstable; a stability config entry was added, then a mutable-field bug appeared because someone put a mutable class under the same wildcard.

questions.promptHtml: How do you see which composables run inside a system trace, and what are the caveats?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you can go from "slow frame" to "this composable" with real tooling.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: By default system traces don't include individual composables. Adding androidx.compose.runtime:runtime-tracing makes composable functions appear as slices in a system trace (Android Studio CPU profiler or Perfetto), with low overhead unlike method tracing. Needs a recent compiler/UI, API 30+ device, and the app must be profileable and non-debuggable for honest timings.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two tracing levels exist: system tracing (cheap, only marked sections) and method tracing (every call, heavy). Composition tracing gives method-level names inside the cheap system trace, because the Compose compiler already injects trace markers (strings) and the runtime-tracing library connects them to the trace backend.

Setup from the docs: implementation("androidx.compose.runtime:runtime-tracing") (version via BOM), API 30+ device. For Macrobenchmark: add androidx.tracing:tracing-perfetto and tracing-perfetto-binary to the benchmark module and pass androidx.benchmark.fullTracing.enable=true. Don't ship tracing-perfetto-binary in production (large).

Reading a trace: find the Choreographer#doFrame slice, look at Recomposer:recompose, then the nested composable slices. Long slice = heavy body; many repeated narrow slices under a single parent = a high-fan-out recomposition.

doFrame
 +- Recomposer:recompose
 |   +- FeedScreen
 |       +- FeedItem x 14   <- all items recomposed on one state change
 +- traversal -> measure/layout   <- separate cost

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Profiling a debuggable build.
  • The tracing strings add APK size and are unobfuscated; strip with the documented -assumenosideeffects rule for production if you care, but then the profiled APK differs from the shipped one.
  • Using recomposition tracing's overhead numbers as truth.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. System vs method trace? → System is low overhead, section-based; method is every call and distorts timing.
  2. Why do your composable slices disappear? → Missing runtime-tracing dependency, or older device than API 30.
  3. How would you add custom sections? → androidx.tracing.trace("name") { } around heavy non-composable code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use Android Studio profiler." Senior: uses system trace plus runtime-tracing, correlates composable slices with doFrame deadline and render thread, and uses the Macrobenchmark-captured trace for repeatability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A trace showed rememberAsyncImagePainter-style setup running per item in composition; the fix was moving it to a pre-built request in the state holder.

questions.promptHtml: What do baseline profiles do for a Compose app, and what do they not fix?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common startup question; checks understanding of ART compilation, not memorized "30% faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A baseline profile is a list of classes and methods critical to user journeys, shipped in the APK so ART AOT-compiles them at install instead of interpreting/JIT-ing on first run. Compose is a library, so without it Compose code is slow on first launch and first use of each feature. Compose ships a default profile for its own code; you add an app profile for your journeys. It fixes cold-path code execution speed, not slow I/O, bad recomposition, or main-thread blocking.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Android platform code is precompiled; library code isn't. On a fresh install or update, the app starts with little compiled code, so startup and first scroll spend time in the interpreter and JIT. A profile moves the hot code to AOT. The docs say about 30% faster code execution from first launch (their figure, journey-dependent); a recent Android Developers Blog post reports Trello at 25% startup reduction and Meta "up to 40%" in metrics (vendor-reported, treat as illustrative).

Workflow: write a Macrobenchmark BaselineProfileRule generator that drives your critical journeys (cold start, first scroll of home feed), generate baseline-prof.txt, ship with release, verify with Macrobenchmark CompilationMode.None() vs Partial(BaselineProfileMode.Require).

@get:Rule val rule = BaselineProfileRule()

@Test fun generate() = rule.collect(packageName = "com.example.app") {
    pressHome()
    startActivityAndWait()
    device.findObject(By.res("feed")).fling(Direction.DOWN)
}

Does not fix: main-thread I/O, recomposition storms, huge bitmaps, layout depth. Profiles only matter on the compiled paths; dynamic content isn't a factor.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Profile covers only cold start; first scroll of feed still janky.
  • Not re-generating after big refactors (profile rules are by class/method name; R8 renaming must match, generate against the minified build).
  • Assuming it helps debug builds.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you prove it helped? → Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric and FrameTimingMetric with and without CompilationMode.
  2. Cloud profiles vs baseline profiles? → Play Cloud Profiles arrive after enough users and some days; baseline is available from first install.
  3. Does it matter beyond startup? → Yes, first-use jank of a feature (first bottom sheet, first navigation), if included in the journey.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Makes startup faster." Senior: explains JIT vs AOT, why Compose-as-library needs it, covers journeys beyond startup, and verifies with compilation-mode benchmarks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team measured p50 cold start improvement but jank in first checkout screen remained; the checkout journey wasn't in the profile generator.

questions.promptHtml: What does "defer state reads" mean, and which modifiers help?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The highest-leverage Compose perf idea: reading state in a later phase skips earlier phases.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compose has three phases: composition, layout, draw. Where you read a State decides which phases re-run. If I read a scroll offset or animated color inside the composable body and pass it as a value, composition re-runs every frame. If I pass a lambda (() -> Int) and read it inside Modifier.offset { }, graphicsLayer { } or drawBehind { }, only layout or draw re-runs and composition is skipped entirely.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reads are tracked by the snapshot system and invalidate whatever scope/phase was active at read time.

read in composable body    -> invalidates recomposition scope -> compose + layout + draw
read in layout lambda      -> invalidates layout only         -> layout + draw
read in draw lambda        -> invalidates draw only           -> draw

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: state read in composition at the parent
Title(snack, scroll.value)            // every pixel scrolled recomposes the scope
Column(Modifier.offset(y = scroll.toDp()))

// Better: provider lambda, read in layout
Title(snack) { scroll.value }
Column(Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, scrollProvider()) })

// Draw-phase color
val color by animateColorAsState(target)
Box(Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(color) })

The official guidance: be suspicious if you recompose just to re-layout or redraw; use lambda-based modifiers for frequently changing values.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the lambda but reading the state eagerly outside it (val v = state.value; Modifier.offset { v }) which defeats the point.
  • Wrapping everything in lambdas, including values that change rarely.
  • Expecting Modifier.offset(x, y) (Dp overload) to defer reads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which modifiers read in which phase? → offset {}/layout {} in layout; drawBehind, drawWithContent, graphicsLayer {} in draw (graphicsLayer lambda runs in draw/layer update).
  2. Is Modifier.alpha(x) deferred? → The value overload is read in composition; use graphicsLayer { alpha = x }.
  3. How does this relate to Animatable? → Animation values read in draw lambdas avoid recomposition per frame.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use remember and keys." Senior: reasons about which phase a read lands in and picks the modifier that skips phases, verifying in a trace that composition slices vanish.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A collapsing toolbar recomposed the full detail screen per scroll pixel; moving the read into offset {} removed composition slices from scroll frames.

questions.promptHtml: Why do key and contentType matter for LazyColumn performance?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundational list trap that also affects state correctness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Without key, Compose identifies items by position. If an item moves (new item inserted at top), every item below shifts index, so Compose treats them as changed and recomposes them, and item state (remember) sticks to positions, not data. A stable unique key lets Compose track items by identity and move them. contentType lets Compose reuse composition slots only between items with the same structure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lazy layouts compose only visible items plus prefetch and retain slots for reuse. The key identifies the item across data changes; also used by rememberSaveable inside items, so keys must be Bundle-saveable (Int/Long/String; never index or hashCode()).

LazyColumn {
    items(items = notes, key = { it.id }, contentType = { it.type }) { note ->
        NoteRow(note)
    }
}

Insert at top with no key: all N visible rows get new data at their position, recompose. With key: only the new row composes; others shift. contentType: reusing a slot from a differently shaped item forces most nodes to be recreated; same type reuses node structure and just updates parameters.

Other docs-listed guidance: use itemsIndexed instead of indexOf inside items (O(N^2) otherwise), hoist shared CompositionLocal reads above the list, and use plain Column for small bounded lists.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the list index or a non-unique field as the key (crash on duplicates: "Key was already used").
  • Using a non-saveable key (e.g., a custom object) and crashing on state save.
  • Mixing very different item types without contentType.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens on duplicate keys? → Runtime IllegalArgumentException for a duplicate key.
  2. Does a key avoid recomposition entirely for moved items? → It avoids recomposing unchanged moved items if their params are equal (skippable).
  3. Where do item states go when key changes? → Lost; a new key is a new item.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Keys for performance." Senior: also covers state correctness, saveable-key requirement, contentType slot reuse, and verifies via counts after an insert-at-top test.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat list without keys recomposed every visible bubble on each incoming message and also swapped expanded states between rows.

questions.contextHtml:
A settings screen has 40 rows (toggles, sliders). Dragging a brightness slider drops to ~35 fps on a mid-range device (6 GB RAM, 60 Hz). Layout Inspector shows every row recomposing on every slider tick. The team says "we added @Immutable to the state class and it didn't help." Code (Kotlin 2.0.20, strong skipping default):

data class SettingsUiState(val brightness: Float, val notifications: Boolean, val items: List<Row>)

@Composable
fun SettingsScreen(vm: SettingsViewModel) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    Column {
        BrightnessSlider(state.brightness) { vm.setBrightness(it) }
        state.items.forEach { row -> SettingRow(row, state) }   // passes whole state
    }
}

@Composable
fun SettingRow(row: Row, state: SettingsUiState) { /* uses row only */ }

Red herring: the ViewModel exposes a StateFlow correctly and the app is a release build.
questions.promptHtml: Why does everything recompose and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add @Stable or ImmutableList everywhere." That ignores that every tick produces a new SettingsUiState instance, so every consumer taking state sees a changed parameter regardless of stability.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this a release build (rules out debug noise)? Does items change per tick (it shouldn't)? Is the slider value in the same state object as rows? What is the frame time in a trace, not just counts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pass row only, not state, to rows; hold the slider value locally while dragging.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SettingRow takes the whole state, which changes each tick: all rows get unequal params. (b) The slider state lives in the same object as everything else. (c) Lambda allocation per row (memoized under strong skipping, so lower). (d) @Immutable irrelevant: equality fails because the value differs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector reset counts and drag; compiler report to confirm rows are skippable; system trace with runtime-tracing to see 40 SettingRow slices per frame.
  5. Root cause: A frequently changing parameter was passed to many children. Skipping compares params; state differs on every tick, so no row skips.
  6. Fix: Pass only what each row needs; split the slider's transient value out.
@Composable
fun SettingsScreen(vm: SettingsViewModel) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    Column {
        var dragging by remember { mutableFloatStateOf(state.brightness) }
        BrightnessSlider(dragging, onChange = { dragging = it }, onFinished = { vm.setBrightness(dragging) })
        state.items.forEach { row -> key(row.id) { SettingRow(row) } }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Review rule: don't pass screen-wide state to leaf composables; compiler-report diff in CI; benchmark of a drag.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrap rows in derivedStateOf or annotate everything; the data flow was the bug. Local drag state means the VM sees only the final value (fine here, wrong if other UI must live-preview).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if brightness must apply live to the window? → Throttle VM writes (e.g., every 50 ms) or apply the window attribute in a side effect from local state.
  • Would @Immutable on SettingsUiState fix it? → No; instance changes per tick, equals() is false.
  • Could a lazy list help? → Only for 40 rows if off-screen; doesn't fix the shared-param problem.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A settings screen passed an AppState blob to every row for "convenience". One toggle recomposed 60 rows; narrowing parameters cut main-thread frame time from 22 ms to 6 ms on the test device.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Compose, adds annotations everywhere.
  • Hire: identifies whole-state param, narrows parameters, verifies with counts.
  • Strong hire: separates transient UI state, explains that stability is irrelevant when values truly differ, adds benchmark guard and review rule.

questions.promptHtml: How do you benchmark scrolling performance of a Compose screen with Macrobenchmark, and which metrics matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Proves you can turn "feels janky" into a repeatable number.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I write a MacrobenchmarkRule.measureRepeated test against a non-debuggable, profileable build, with FrameTimingMetric, a fixed compilation mode, StartupMode.WARM or a navigate-first setup, and a deterministic scroll (fling a tagged list). I compare frameDurationCpuMs P50/P90/P95/P99 and frameOverrunMs between builds. Run on a real device, many iterations, in CI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
@get:Rule val rule = MacrobenchmarkRule()

@Test fun scroll() = rule.measureRepeated(
    packageName = "com.example.app",
    metrics = listOf(FrameTimingMetric()),
    compilationMode = CompilationMode.Partial(),
    iterations = 10,
    startupMode = StartupMode.WARM,
    setupBlock = { pressHome(); startActivityAndWait() }
) {
    val list = device.findObject(By.res("feed"))
    list.setGestureMargin(device.displayWidth / 5)
    list.fling(Direction.DOWN)
    device.waitForIdle()
}

For Compose, expose the list through Modifier.semantics { testTagsAsResourceId = true } plus testTag("feed") so UiAutomator finds it. FrameTimingMetric reports frameDurationCpuMs (UI+RenderThread CPU time per frame) and, on API 31+, frameOverrunMs (negative = slack, positive = missed deadline).

Reading results: the tail (P95/P99) shows jank; P50 shows typical cost. Compare variants (before/after change; CompilationMode.None vs Partial) in the same run session; attach the trace the benchmark captures to see composition slices (needs the fullTracing arg and perfetto deps).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Benchmarking a debuggable build or an emulator.
  • Too few iterations; noise swamps a 5% change.
  • Flinging a list that isn't loaded (network); use fixtures.
  • Not pinning compilation mode, so JIT warm-up varies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Macrobenchmark vs Microbenchmark? → Macro measures the whole app out of process (startup, scroll); micro measures a function in a loop in process.
  2. Why testTagsAsResourceId? → UiAutomator sees resource IDs, not Compose tags, unless exposed.
  3. Why frameOverrunMs? → It shows how far past the deadline a frame landed, which separates "slightly late" from "badly late".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Write a benchmark." Senior: controls compilation mode, device tier, iterations, data fixtures, reports tail percentiles, and wires it into CI with regression thresholds.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "free" refactor to the feed item layout looked fine locally; the benchmark showed P99 frame time up 4 ms, caught before release.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use JankStats instead of (or alongside) Macrobenchmark for a Compose app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates lab measurement from field telemetry and tests API knowledge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Macrobenchmark is lab testing: controlled, repeatable, pre-release. JankStats runs in production: it gets per-frame data via FrameMetrics (API 24+), flags jank using a heuristic, and attaches UI state ("screen = Feed, list = scrolling") so I can aggregate jank by screen across real devices. I use Macrobenchmark to gate regressions and JankStats to find where real users hurt.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
JankStats (androidx.metrics:metrics-performance) wraps FrameMetrics on API 24+ (OnPreDrawListener earlier). You create it per Window and receive FrameData per frame: isJank, frameDurationUiNanos, frameStartNanos, states; on API 31+ extra data like frameOverrunNanos. By default jank is a frame taking twice the refresh interval; jankHeuristicMultiplier adjusts it.

The PerformanceMetricsState API lets you tag frames: in Compose, report scrolling from a side effect, not composition:

val holder = remember(view) { PerformanceMetricsState.getHolderForHierarchy(view) }
LaunchedEffect(holder, listState) {
    snapshotFlow { listState.isScrollInProgress }.collect { scrolling ->
        if (scrolling) holder.state?.putState("FeedList", "Scrolling")
        else holder.state?.removeState("FeedList")
    }
}

Constraints from docs: the listener runs on a background FrameMetrics thread (API 24+), FrameData is reused (copy what you keep), and keep the callback fast. Aggregate and upload batches, not per frame.

Macrobenchmark JankStats
Where CI/device lab production
Controlled yes no
Context scripted journey app state tags
Output percentiles per build jank rate by screen/device

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting state with a generic key ("List") for many lists.
  • Uploading per-frame data (battery, size).
  • Treating field jank rate as comparable across device classes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just use dumpsys gfxinfo? → Local only; not telemetry.
  2. How do you avoid recomposition from reporting state? → Use LaunchedEffect + snapshotFlow, not state reads in composition.
  3. How would you alert? → Percent of janky frames per screen per app version and device bucket, with a threshold on regression.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "JankStats detects jank." Senior: positions it in the measurement stack, handles tagging cost and aggregation, and slices by device class and version.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Field JankStats data showed jank concentrated on one screen on 3 GB devices, which lab tests on a flagship never reproduced.

questions.contextHtml:
A search screen (40k DAU) gets reviews: "typing lags." On a low-end device (3 GB RAM, API 29), keystrokes appear after ~250 ms. The release build is affected. Code:

@Composable
fun SearchScreen(vm: SearchViewModel) {
    val query by vm.query.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()   // StateFlow<String>
    val results by vm.results.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    Column {
        TextField(value = query, onValueChange = { vm.onQuery(it) })
        ResultList(results.filter { it.title.contains(query, true) }.sortedBy { it.score })
    }
}
// ViewModel
fun onQuery(q: String) { viewModelScope.launch { delay(50); _query.value = q } }

Trace: main thread frames 28-40 ms during typing; SearchScreen slice ~14 ms per keystroke.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Debounce more." The lag is partly self-inflicted by the async round trip and by heavy work on every keystroke in composition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many results (size N)? Is results already filtered server-side? Which Compose BOM? Does TextField use the value overload with state hoisted to a StateFlow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the delay from the field's write path; filter off the main thread.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Hoisting the text through a StateFlow with launch + delay adds async hops; the text field state updates a frame late, causing cursor/IME desync and visible lag. (b) filter + sortedBy over N items run in composition on every keystroke. (c) ResultList takes a new list each pass, so it recomposes fully. (d) Red herring: image loading.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace: SearchScreen slice length; count items N; Layout Inspector counts on rows during typing.
  5. Root cause: Text state must update synchronously on the main thread; async set via the ViewModel and O(N log N) work in composition per keystroke blow the frame budget.
  6. Fix: Keep the text in Compose-owned state (rememberTextFieldState in newer foundation, or rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf }), push debounced queries to the VM, compute results in the VM on Dispatchers.Default.
var text by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
    snapshotFlow { text }.debounce(150).collectLatest { vm.search(it) }
}
TextField(value = text, onValueChange = { text = it })
ResultList(results) // already filtered and sorted in the ViewModel
  1. Prevention: Benchmark typing with TextField via FrameTimingMetric and a UI test; code review rule: no collection transforms in composable bodies.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not add remember(query) around the filter (still runs per keystroke on main); not pre-optimize the row. Local text state means VM isn't the single source of truth for the field; that's a deliberate exception for the transient input.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is async text state a bug and not just lag? → onValueChange must update synchronously or the IME composition (cursor, selection, composing region) is overwritten.
  • What if search must be instant for 5k local items? → Index off-main in VM, StateFlow of results, collectLatest.
  • How does TextFieldState change things? → The newer state-based API (verify your foundation version) keeps edit state inside Compose and avoids this class of desync.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A product search did delay + VM round trip for the text value; Korean/Japanese IME input broke (composition cancelled) on low-end devices until text state stayed in the composable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only increases debounce.
  • Hire: identifies main-thread filtering and the async text hoist.
  • Strong hire: explains IME synchronous-state contract, moves work to VM, adds measurement.

questions.contextHtml:
A LazyColumn shows a "back to top" FAB. QA reports scrolling stutters when the FAB logic is present (about 52 fps vs 60 without it). Code:

@Composable
fun Feed(items: List<Item>) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val showFab = remember(listState.firstVisibleItemIndex) {
        derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 }
    }.value
    LazyColumn(state = listState) { items(items, key = { it.id }) { ItemRow(it) } }
    if (showFab) ScrollToTop()
}

Layout Inspector: Feed recomposes on every item boundary scrolled, and its children re-evaluate.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and explain why it hurts.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "derivedStateOf is expensive, remove it." It's the placement of reads that's wrong.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Compose runtime version (1.13+ has computedStateOf per docs, verify)? Are items skippable? Does ItemRow read other state?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the key from remember.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) firstVisibleItemIndex is read in composition as a remember key, so Feed invalidates every time the index changes and a new DerivedState is created each time, defeating its purpose. (b) .value read at the top scope rather than where used. (c) Recomposing the parent re-runs items lambda setup.
  4. How I'd verify each: Counts on Feed; trace shows Feed slice per boundary; fix and re-measure.
  5. Root cause: The docs warn: don't pass the snapshot values read inside derivedStateOf as remember keys; it recreates the DerivedState on every change and prevents skipping. The key read is itself the scroll-state read.
  6. Fix:
val showFab by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }
// or on runtime 1.13+: remember { computedStateOf { ... } }  (verify)

Even better, move the if (showFab) into a small composable that reads the state, so only it recomposes. 7. Prevention: Lint/review rule for keys on derived state; test counts while scrolling. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not hold firstVisibleItemIndex in my own state with LaunchedEffect; extra hop and lag. Not use derivedStateOf for trivial reads (like list.size); docs say a plain read is enough when no dampening is needed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• When does derivedStateOf help? → When input changes much more often than the derived output (scroll offset to boolean).
  • When does it hurt? → Output changes as often as input, or cheap reads: pure overhead.
  • Is a lambda () -> Boolean param better? → Yes for deferring: pass the provider so the read happens in the child.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "show scroll-to-top" check using index key made the entire home screen recompose at each row boundary; moving to the keyless derivedStateOf dropped 11 ms/frame of composition during scroll.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "remove derivedStateOf".
  • Hire: spots the key problem and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: explains invalidation, places the read low, and cites when derivation is unnecessary.

questions.promptHtml: With strong skipping on, are unstable parameters still a performance problem? When?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Distinguishes people repeating 2022 advice ("everything must be stable") from those who know the current model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With strong skipping (default since Kotlin 2.0.20), all restartable composables are skippable, and unstable params are compared by instance (===) while stable ones use equals(). So an unstable List isn't a problem if the same instance is passed. It becomes a problem when a new but equal instance is allocated every emission/recomposition (e.g., .map {} in the ViewModel or in composition), because === fails.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules from the docs: lambdas with unstable captures are memoized with remember keyed on captures (compared by the same rules); @NonSkippableComposable opts out; @DontMemoize prevents lambda memoization.

Param type   Compare   Skips when
stable       equals()  values equal
unstable     ===       same instance

Where it still bites:

  1. New instance each time: val sorted = items.sortedBy{} in a composable body without remember; .map in a StateFlow transform that re-emits on any change of unrelated state.
  2. Pre-2.0.20 builds (or modules with the old compiler): unstable param means non-skippable; enable the option explicitly (enableStrongSkippingMode = true).
  3. Library classes allocated fresh per emission where equals() would have matched.

Fixes in order: keep instance identity (cache in VM, remember(input)), then @Immutable/@Stable on small flat classes with cheap equals(), then config file entries. The docs caution that annotating collection holders or using ImmutableList causes element-by-element equals() per pass, which can cost more than recomposing in big lazy lists.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Allocates a new List every recomposition -> child never skips
Row(items.filter { it.visible })
// Preserve identity
val visible = remember(items) { items.filter { it.visible } }
Row(visible)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping everything in ImmutableList by habit.
  • Annotating a class @Stable that holds MutableList: contract broken, stale UI.
  • Believing lambdas are unstable (the compiler always considers them stable; the issue was non-memoization).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Kotlin 2.0 change inference? → Yes, the compiler plugin ships with Kotlin 2.0+, strong skipping default from 2.0.20; verify per module.
  2. How do you spot a fresh instance each emission? → Log System.identityHashCode in dev or trace recompositions of children.
  3. What if the child must run equals() anyway? → Annotate the small class; accept the compare cost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Make all classes stable." Senior: "Identity is the contract; keep instances stable, annotate only small cheap-equals classes."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mapper in the VM rebuilt the whole UI list on a unrelated flag change; every row recomposed until the mapping was cached.

questions.contextHtml: A social feed (2.5M DAU, 40% on devices with 3-4 GB RAM) got a release that shipped a new card layout. Post-release: P95 frame time on feed scroll went from 11 ms to 24 ms at 60 Hz (16.6 ms budget); janky-frame rate from 3% to 14% (JankStats, field). Crash rate unchanged; ANR unchanged. Android vitals shows "excessive slow frames" on 3 GB devices only. The PR also bumped Compose BOM and added a Modifier.shadow to cards, added a 6-image grid inside the card, and moved the feed to StateFlow<List<Post>> rebuilt on every like.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the investigation and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back everything" without isolation, or "add remember". No method.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which exact change correlates (staged rollout %)? Is jank during scroll or after a like? Which device buckets? Does LazyColumn use key/contentType? Is the baseline profile regenerated for the new layout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt rollout, flag off the new card via remote config if possible, else rollback; keep the BOM bump separate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) card composition cost (6-image grid, multiple nested Layouts) lands in the prefetch/first-appear frame; (b) Modifier.shadow on every card (blur cost on GPU on low-end); (c) list rebuilt per like with no keys, recomposing every visible item; (d) baseline profile stale, so new code is JIT'd (first-scroll only); (e) BOM bump regression (least likely, other apps unaffected).
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark on a 3 GB device with FrameTimingMetric, A/B build per change; system trace with composition tracing: look for long FeedCard slices, then render thread for shadow draw; Layout Inspector counts after a like; compiler report on card params; re-run with CompilationMode.Full to isolate JIT.
  5. Root cause (example finding): Item composition ~9 ms per new card on low-end (grid of 6 AsyncImage with sizing math in composition) plus whole-list recomposition on like (no keys, new list instances). Shadows added ~3 ms GPU per frame on that GPU class.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove/replace shadow with a flat elevation approximation, add key and contentType, update only the changed post (copy the list with one changed element, keep other instances). Long-term: reduce the grid to a single composited layout or Canvas, pre-size images, move image requests into the item state holder, regenerate baseline profile with a feed scroll journey, consider LazyLayoutCacheWindow for prefetch (verify version).
LazyColumn {
    items(posts, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "post" }) { PostCard(it) }
}
  1. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll gate on a low-tier device in CI; JankStats alert on jank% by screen/device; compiler report diff; design review for per-item cost budget.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blanket @Immutable; not drop images; no new library. Dropping shadows changes design; negotiate with design using measured cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Jank only for the first 2 seconds of scroll? → JIT/baseline profile or cold image decode.
  • Jank on a like tap only? → Whole-list recomposition; fix keys and update one element.
  • How would pausable composition (Compose 1.9/1.10 lazy prefetch, per Android blog) help? → Spreads heavy item composition over frames; confirm version and benchmark.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A card redesign added nested blur and a 6-image grid; benchmark on a 3 GB device found 8 ms composition per card. Cutting layout nodes by half and caching image requests brought janky frames back to under 4%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random fixes without measurement.
  • Hire: isolates changes, uses trace/benchmark, fixes keys.
  • Strong hire: separates composition/GPU/JIT causes, device-tiered gates and field alerting.

questions.promptHtml: Skipping is "free", right? When does making a composable skippable make things slower?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the runtime cost model rather than cargo-cult optimization.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. Every parameter of a skippable composable is stored in the slot table and compared on each recomposition pass. If equals() is expensive (large collections, ImmutableList of thousands of items) or the composable is trivial, the compare can cost more than just recomposing. Deferring reads to layout/draw usually beats adding skipping.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Skippable function = generated code that checks $changed bits and calls equals()/=== per parameter before executing the body. Stable parameters use equals(): for a data class with a List of 5,000 items annotated stable, each pass compares up to 5,000 elements (O(n)), and doubles if passed down again (the docs show an ImmutableList example compared twice: in the parent's equals and the child's).

Heuristics from the docs:

  • Don't force skippability for composables that rarely recompose, that only call skippable composables, or that take many params with costly equals().
  • @NonRestartableComposable / @NonSkippableComposable exist for hot, tiny composables.
  • Prefer stable instance reuse over forcing structural equality for collections in lazy layouts.
Parent recompose -> child skippable: compare k params
   cheap equals: ~ns each      -> skip wins
   data class with List<10k> @Stable: O(n) -> may cost more than the child body

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting recompositions as the metric.
  • Replacing all List with ImmutableList and adding @Immutable to list-holding models.
  • Making a 3-line leaf skippable with 8 parameters.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to measure it? → Trace slices for both paths; Macrobenchmark with and without the annotation.
  2. Which is better: === on a cached list or equals() on an immutable one? → Cached identity, if you can preserve it.
  3. Should Modifier params be a concern? → Modifier comparison runs equals on the chain; chains with many elements cost a bit; extract static modifiers when cheap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Skipping saves work." Senior: "Skipping trades work for compare cost; I use it where body cost >> compare cost, and I defer reads for fast-changing values."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team annotating FeedState stable (holding 800 posts) increased scroll jank; removing the annotation and caching the list in the VM cut frame time.

questions.promptHtml: Give me a catalogue of things that should never run in a composable body, and where each goes instead.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real production traps in one list; tests judgment, not recall.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Composition can run per frame, so anything blocking, allocating a lot, or side-effecting is wrong there: sorting/filtering collections, regex/date formatting, JSON parsing, I/O, creating heavy objects (formatters, Paint, painters), launching coroutines directly, and writing state. They go to remember, the ViewModel, produceState/effects, or off the main thread.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Trap Why bad Instead
list.sortedBy{} / filter per pass O(n log n) each recompose VM or remember(list, key)
SimpleDateFormat/NumberFormat creation allocation + locale lookup remember once
Regex(...) in body compile each time top-level val
State write in body backwards write loop write in events/effects
Reading LocalContext.current many times per item cheap per call, but hoist for lazy items (docs) read above list
Disk/DB/network call blocks main VM + flow
Brush/Path creation in draw each frame allocation per frame remember/drawWithCache
New lambda capturing unstable values (pre strong-skipping) defeats skipping remember or enable strong skipping 
val formatter = remember { DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("d MMM") }
val text = remember(date) { formatter.format(date) }

Note the docs caution: remember keys are compared with equals() on every pass; remember an expensive thing, not a cheap getter, and don't key on a big collection for a cheap calculation.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• remember everything including x + 1.
  • Using remember(list) and mutating the list in place (never invalidates).
  • Doing work in LaunchedEffect(Unit) that should be in the VM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. drawWithCache use? → Allocate path/brush once per size change, reuse in draw.
  2. Why not async in composition? → Side effect in composition; may run multiple times, not cancelled with the scope; use effects.
  3. Where is the line for work in remember? → If it's more than ~1 ms on a low-end device or O(n) with large n, it belongs off the main thread.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use remember." Senior: lists what moves off main, notes remember's own compare cost, and uses drawWithCache.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Regex per row for hashtag highlighting in a chat list was the top slice in the trace; moving it to a top-level val and per-message memoization removed it.

questions.contextHtml:
After a refactor, a "cart badge" screen drains battery: CPU stays ~35% on a still screen, Perfetto shows Recomposer:recompose every frame with nothing changing. Only on screens using this composable:

@Composable
fun CartBadge(items: List<CartItem>) {
    var total by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
    Text("Total: $total")
    total = items.sumOf { it.price * it.qty }     // "keep it in sync"
}

No crash, no log, app looks fine. Same code in a debug build produces occasional "Composition recomposed ... times" style warnings only sometimes (do not rely on them).
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose it and fix it properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in LaunchedEffect" without understanding why the loop happens, or "Compose is buggy."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the screen idle yet recomposing (yes)? Did the change introduce a state write in body? Is items changing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Compute total without state.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) State written after being read in the same composition (backwards write) so it invalidates itself. (b) Infinite animation elsewhere. (c) A flow emitting identical values. I check (a) first because recompose-per-frame with no input matches it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Recomposition counts climbing at idle in Layout Inspector; trace shows CartBadge each frame; remove the write to confirm.
  5. Root cause: total is read by Text, then written later in the same pass. Compose's assumption is that you never write state already read. The write changes total only when the value differs, but the next pass reads again; if the value flips (e.g., derived from changing list identity or non-deterministic) it keeps invalidating. Even when equal, it adds an extra recomposition per change. The docs describe this as recomposing endlessly.
  6. Fix:
@Composable
fun CartBadge(items: List<CartItem>) {
    val total = remember(items) { items.sumOf { it.price * it.qty } }
    Text("Total: $total")
}

Keep derived values derived; write state only from events or effects. 7. Prevention: Review rule: no assignments to state in composable body; use the Compose lint/inspections that flag state writes in composition; idle recomposition test (assert count stable). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not suppress with SideEffect to write state (still extra pass); not derivedStateOf for a trivial sum unless recomputation is expensive and read many times.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not an error? → Writes in composition are allowed; they trigger another recomposition, bounded only by convergence.
  • When is writing state in SideEffect legit? → Publishing to non-Compose objects, not Compose state read in the same tree.
  • How to test? → Compose test with mainClock.autoAdvance; assert recomposition count after idle (see testing question).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "sync" assignment kept one screen's CPU at 30% idle; battery stats flagged it, not crash reports. A deterministic idle test now guards all hot screens.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain why idle recomposition happens.
  • Hire: identifies backwards write, derives value instead.
  • Strong hire: adds idle-recomposition test, explains read/write ordering and lint.

questions.promptHtml: You see a composable recomposing too often but can't tell which state write triggered it. What do you do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Counts say "how many", not "why"; this probes whether you know the newer tooling and the fallback reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use recomposition tracing: with runtime-tracing 1.13+ (docs: BOM 2026.11+, API 29+; verify for your version) a system trace shows state reads and writes next to composable slices, and selecting a state write shows its call stack and a flow arrow to the recomposition it caused. Without it, I reason from reads: find which state the scope read, add temporary logging on writers, and check who writes that state and how often.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism: a recomposition happens because a snapshot state object that a scope read was written and the snapshot applied; the Recomposer invalidates scopes registered as readers. Composition tracing tells you what ran; recomposition tracing adds causality: writer -> invalidated scope.

Capture (docs): run record_recomposition_trace.py -p <package> from the performance-samples repo, interact, stop, open the zip in Perfetto. Overhead is higher than composition tracing: use it to debug, not to measure timings.

Fallback manual method:

// temp: who invalidates me?
SideEffect { Log.d("Recomp", "FeedHeader") }    // frequency only
snapshotFlow { vm.uiState.value.count }.collect { /* log writer rate */ }

Then ask: is the reader at the wrong level (read in a parent body), is the writer high-frequency (scroll, animation, a ticking timer), or is a new instance each emission?

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using recomposition tracing durations to measure performance.
  • Adding Log in composition on release, creating cost.
  • Ignoring that one write can invalidate many scopes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the arrow from write to recompose possible? → Snapshot write observers record which state object was modified and the invalidation links to the reader scope.
  2. What's the next step after finding the writer? → Lower the read (lambda/draw/layout), debounce the writer, or split the state.
  3. Does it work in a Macrobenchmark? → Composition tracing does with fullTracing; recomposition tracing is best for local debugging (verify).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Log in each composable." Senior: uses causal tracing and reasons in snapshot read/write terms.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Recomposition traces showed a 1-second ticker flow updating a timestamp state read at screen root; moving the read into a leaf stopped full-screen recomposition.

questions.promptHtml: What is the performance cost model of modifiers, and why is Modifier.Node preferred over composed {}?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of how custom modifiers affect composition and allocation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Modifier chain is a persistent immutable list; each recomposition may allocate new chain elements and compares chains with equals(). composed {} runs a composable lambda per use, creating remembered state and extra composition work, and it makes modifiers non-skippable-friendly; Modifier.Node (via ModifierNodeElement) creates a lightweight node once, updates it in place through update(), and the runtime diffs elements by equals(). So Node-based modifiers allocate less and don't invoke composition.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Built-in modifiers like padding, background, clickable are implemented on Modifier.Node internally. A custom one:

private class CircleNode(var color: Color) : Modifier.Node(), DrawModifierNode {
    override fun ContentDrawScope.draw() { drawCircle(color); drawContent() }
}
private data class CircleElement(val color: Color) : ModifierNodeElement<CircleNode>() {
    override fun create() = CircleNode(color)
    override fun update(node: CircleNode) { node.color = color }
}
fun Modifier.circle(color: Color) = this then CircleElement(color)

Costs: element creation (cheap, per recomposition); equals() on the element (data class); if equal, no node update. With composed {} the lambda executes in composition for each call site, creating remembered state and inhibiting skipping and tooling (modifier equality always fails for composed). Android docs recommend Node-based modifiers for custom modifiers (verify current guidance on composed deprecation status for your version).

Practical rules: remember modifier chains that are expensive or static; hoist constant modifiers to top-level vals; avoid creating pointerInput blocks with unstable keys that restart per recomposition.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• pointerInput(Unit) capturing stale lambdas (use rememberUpdatedState).
  • Modifier.clickable { } creating lambdas capturing changing values per item (fine under strong skipping if memoized).
  • Making the element a non-data class so equals() never matches.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does an unequal element matter? → update() runs each pass and may invalidate layout/draw.
  2. Where is invalidateDraw called? → In the node's setter when a draw-affecting property changes (DrawModifierNode helpers).
  3. How do you test a custom modifier's cost? → Trace slices and benchmark in a list of 100 items.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Chain order matters." Senior: understands node lifecycle and element equality as the performance contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shimmer composed {} modifier on 30 list rows recomposed constantly; a Node-based version with a draw-phase read removed it from the trace.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants cold start under 1.4 s on a mid-range device (currently P50 2.1 s). The team added a baseline profile generated from a 20-line test that only launches the app to the login screen; Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric improved P50 from 2.4 s to 2.1 s. Real users spend startup in the home feed (first frame of feed at ~3.4 s TTFD). Release uses R8 (full mode) with Compose. App code on first load: 6 feature modules init eagerly in Application.onCreate (~600 ms main thread).
questions.promptHtml: How do you get to 1.4 s and what does the baseline profile contribute?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more rules to the baseline profile" or "move to View system".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which metric: TTID or TTFD (reportFullyDrawn)? Is the user logged in 95% of the time (so login isn't the path)? Device tier? Is R8 on in the benchmark variant?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Extend profile journeys to the authenticated home feed; ship now since it's low risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) profile misses the real journey (home/feed compose code JIT'd); (b) Application.onCreate eager inits dominate; (c) first-frame composition of heavy feed; (d) R8 not applied or keeps too much (red herring if release minify is on).
  4. How I'd verify each: Benchmark with CompilationMode.None vs Partial vs Full to see the headroom; system trace of cold start with composition tracing; Trace sections in Application init; App Startup library lazy-init audit.
  5. Root cause: The profile covered the wrong path, and 600 ms of eager work is independent of AOT. Compose library code is only precompiled by Compose's own profile; your composables aren't unless in your profile.
  6. Fix: Generate a profile that logs in as a fixture user, opens home, scrolls once; run generation against the minified build; defer non-critical SDK inits (App Startup, background threads); call reportFullyDrawn() after first feed content. Reprofile; compare Full as the upper bound.
rule.collect(packageName = "com.example.app", includeInStartupProfile = true) {
    startActivityAndWait()
    device.wait(Until.hasObject(By.res("feed")), 5_000)
    device.findObject(By.res("feed")).fling(Direction.DOWN)
}
  1. Prevention: Startup benchmark in CI with regression threshold; profile regenerated per release; trace-based startup budget.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not include the entire app in the profile (larger APK/install-time compile); not sacrifice correctness by lazy-initializing things needed in first frame. See A6 for the startup playbook.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Profile fixes 40% but target not met? → Remaining is main-thread work and I/O; trace the cold start.
  • Does the Compose default profile cover your code? → No, only Compose library code.
  • Device with Play cloud profile vs local? → Cloud profiles take time to propagate; the baseline profile helps from first install.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A profile built for a splash-only journey gave 5% gain; adding the logged-in home journey plus deferring three SDK inits took cold start from 2.3 s to 1.5 s P50.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes profile is a switch.
  • Hire: aligns profile with the real journey, uses CompilationMode comparisons.
  • Strong hire: also attacks main-thread init, defines TTFD metrics, and CI regression gating.

questions.promptHtml: How do you write an automated test that fails when a screen recomposes too much?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Performance regressions need guardrails; tests whether you can make recomposition observable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In a Compose UI test, I count executions with a counter incremented from a SideEffect (runs after each successful composition of that scope) in the composable under test, drive an interaction, and assert the count. Use composeTestRule.runOnIdle, control the clock, and test a skippable unit with stable inputs. It catches regressions like "typing recomposes the whole form". It's a guard, not a timing measure; pair it with Macrobenchmark.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
@get:Rule val rule = createComposeRule()

@Test fun togglingOneRow_doesNotRecomposeOthers() {
    val counts = mutableMapOf<Int, Int>()
    rule.setContent {
        var checked by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
        Column {
            Row(Modifier.testTag("row0").clickable { checked = !checked }) { Text("$checked") }
            Counted(1, counts) { Static() }
        }
    }
    val before = counts[1]
    rule.onNodeWithTag("row0").performClick()
    rule.waitForIdle()
    assertEquals(before, counts[1])
}

@Composable fun Counted(id: Int, counts: MutableMap<Int, Int>, content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    SideEffect { counts[id] = (counts[id] ?: 0) + 1 }
    content()
}

Caveats: SideEffect inside the same scope runs when that scope recomposes, so put it in the composable you assert about. Tests run with the test dispatcher and no real frames; use mainClock to advance. Assertions on exact counts can be brittle across Compose versions: assert "does not increase" or a bounded number. An idle test: mainClock.autoAdvance = false, advance a few frames, assert no recompositions.

Libraries exist (e.g. recomposition-highlighter style tools) but be careful about adding dependencies; the SideEffect counter is enough.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting in the lambda param instead of the composable body.
  • Asserting exact numbers copied from a run.
  • Expecting tests to prove frame-time improvements.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why SideEffect, not a println? → println runs during composition (may run speculatively/ multiple times); SideEffect runs after commit.
  2. How to test an idle screen? → Disable autoAdvance, advance clock, assert count stable (catches backwards writes).
  3. Where do these tests run? → Instrumented or Robolectric (verify Compose support in your setup); keep them in the module with the composable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "UI tests check text." Senior: encodes performance invariants (no recomposition at idle, only changed row recomposes) as tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An idle recomposition test caught a clock ticker state read at the root before release.

questions.subtopic: First-scroll jank in a heavy item
questions.contextHtml: A product detail screen has a LazyColumn of 12 items; the 4th item is a "specs" card with a 200-row table built using nested Rows/Columns and a text-heavy layout. Scrolling to it drops 8-10 frames on a mid-range device (P99 frame 48 ms); subsequent scrolls are fine. Release build, baseline profile present. Trace: SpecsCard composition 22 ms + measure 11 ms in one frame on the UI thread.
questions.promptHtml: What do you try, in order, and how do you verify?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it a RecyclerView." or "Add remember."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the table be virtualized (is it inherently 200 rows)? Does it need to be in the same lazy list? Static content? Compose version (prefetch behaviors differ)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Collapse by default ("show more") to cut initial composition.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one huge item composes in a single frame; prefetch only composes one item ahead (default) and can't finish in the idle slice; (b) text measurement cost (200 Text nodes); (c) intrinsic measurements in rows; (d) Column of 200 children instead of lazy.
  4. How I'd verify each: Composition tracing: per-node cost; measure phase slice; try LazyLayoutCacheWindow (verify API/version) and check whether the cost moves off the critical frame.
  5. Root cause: A single item whose composition+measure exceeds the frame budget; prefetching can't help if the item cost exceeds idle time. Pausable composition for lazy prefetch (introduced in Compose 1.9 and default for lazy prefetch in 1.10 per the Android Developers Blog; verify) helps only when the item can be split across frames.
  6. Fix: Break the table into lazy items (each row an item or a small chunk) so cost spreads; use Text with simpler layout (single Text with AnnotatedString columns or a Canvas-drawn table) for static content; enlarge prefetch window for big items; warm text via background text prefetch (1.9+, verify).
LazyColumn(state = listState /* consider LazyLayoutCacheWindow per docs */) {
    items(specRows, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "spec" }) { SpecRow(it) }
}
  1. Prevention: Per-item cost budget in design review; scroll benchmark covering the heavy screen.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not nest a lazy list inside a scroll container (infinite height crash risk); not hide the cost with a placeholder only.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Spec table must be one visual card? → Use item { } per section with card shape drawn via drawBehind/clip per chunk.
  • Why not just cache composition? → Composition result can't be cached across lazy disposal; state is retained only via rememberSaveable/keys.
  • What about Column(Modifier.verticalScroll)? → Composes everything up front; worse for 200 rows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A spec sheet in one item took 30 ms to compose; splitting into 20 row items removed the stall at the cost of slightly more nodes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random micro-optimizations.
  • Hire: splits into smaller lazy items and traces.
  • Strong hire: explains prefetch limits and tradeoffs, measures before/after.

questions.contextHtml: After a recomposition scare, a team spent two sprints "making everything stable": replaced all List with ImmutableList, added @Immutable to 120 UI model classes (some holding MutableList and var fields), added kotlin.collections.* to stability_config.conf, and wrapped many composables in remember. After release: scroll jank on the main feed worsened (P95 frame 13 ms to 19 ms), and two bugs: a cart screen not updating after edit, and a tag list showing stale items. Rollback restored jank.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened and what policy replaces it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Annotations are bad, ban them." Or blames the team without mechanisms.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which changes shipped together? Was there a baseline benchmark before? Which models had var fields? Kotlin version/strong skipping state?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert annotations on mutable classes (correctness bugs first), then collection-config rule (perf).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) @Immutable on mutable classes: compose skipped recompositions because equals() stayed true after in-place mutation, causing stale UI (the contract violation the docs warn about). (b) ImmutableList and collection stability config: per-element equals() on each pass, costly in feed items, double compares when nested in data classes. (c) Excess remember with big keys (equals() cost). (d) Some real gains offset by these.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce the stale bugs with a test; benchmark per change (revert collection config only); trace compares; compiler reports showing now-stable collection holder classes.
  5. Root cause: Process failure: optimizing a metric (stability counts) rather than frame time, no benchmark gate, and annotations used as an override without owning the contract.
  6. Fix: Re-enable strong skipping defaults; remove collection stability config; keep instance identity via VM caching; keep @Immutable only on small immutable (all val, immutable types) classes from non-Compose modules that are re-allocated; fix mutable models to use immutable updates.
  7. Prevention: Policy: no optimization PR without a benchmark before/after; code review checklist for annotations (must be truly immutable; cheap equals); CI Macrobenchmark; compiler report diff reviewed only for hot composables.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not ban ImmutableList outright (useful when identity can't be preserved and benchmarks agree); not freeze work on stability; instead time-box it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you find all contract-violating @Immutable classes? → Grep for @Immutable classes with var or mutable collection fields; add a detekt/lint rule.
  • Would you keep any remember changes? → Those caching expensive work; drop remember over cheap derived values.
  • How to convince management? → Show before/after benchmark graphs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "stability sprint" shipped 120 annotations; two stale-UI bugs came from classes with var fields. The review produced a rule: every perf PR links a benchmark delta.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames individuals or tools.
  • Hire: identifies contract violation and equals cost.
  • Strong hire: builds benchmark-gated policy, detection lint, and balanced guidance.

questions.contextHtml: A 30-engineer Android team ships Compose weekly. Three jank regressions reached production this quarter (all found via reviews). Budget: CI can spend 25 minutes per PR on one physical low-tier device lab device (shared) and emulators; flakiness tolerance is low. Leadership wants "no more jank regressions" without blocking every PR.
questions.promptHtml: Design the regression-prevention system.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run Macrobenchmark on every PR" ignoring flakiness, lab capacity and noise.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which journeys matter (feed scroll, checkout)? Existing device lab? Acceptable regression threshold? Do we have field jank telemetry?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a nightly Macrobenchmark on the feed with a Slack alert, before building gating.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what to guard): (a) scroll frame timing on hot screens; (b) startup; (c) idle recomposition; (d) APK size/baseline profile freshness.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric, StartupTimingMetric; Compose idle recomposition tests; JankStats field jank per screen/version.
  5. Root cause of past misses: No automated measurement; perf only known post-release.
  6. Fix (design): Tiered gates: (1) every PR: fast unit/UI tests including idle-recomposition invariants, compiler-report diff for annotated hot composables (cheap); (2) PRs touching feed/perf-labeled modules: Macrobenchmark on a lab device, 10+ iterations, compare P95 vs baseline from main with noise threshold (e.g., regress >10% fails after repeat); (3) nightly full journey benchmarks with trend graph; (4) field: JankStats jank-rate by screen/device/version with alerts and staged rollout halts.
  7. Prevention: Own baselines per device model; pin CPU/thermal where possible; quarantine flaky benchmarks; store results over time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not gate on emulator numbers; not make all PRs wait for lab; accept some regressions escape to nightly (cheaper than blocked merges).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Benchmark noise 8%? → Use more iterations, compare distributions, set threshold above noise, rerun on failure.
  • Cost of device farm? → Prioritize paths touched via CODEOWNERS labels.
  • Field vs lab disagree? → Trust field for prevalence, lab for diagnosis.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly benchmark graph caught a feed regression three days after merge; bisecting between two nightly builds took an hour instead of a week of review complaints.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "run benchmarks on every PR".
  • Hire: tiered gates and thresholds.
  • Strong hire: combines lab, nightly, field telemetry, noise handling and ownership.
